S5: - The lunar month (29.5 days) is two days longer than the Moon's trip around the sky (27.3 days), because the Earth itself is moving (NASA StarChild). - The Sun moves at about 230 km/s around the galaxy, one circuit in about 230 million years (NASA StarChild). - The crescent the verse compares to a dried date stalk is the same shape whose sighting begins each Islamic month.

Each point is tied to a phrase in the verses. - **"We have determined for it phases" (36:39).** [Established] The Moon goes once around the sky relative to the stars "in about 27.3 days", but "takes 29.5 days to return to the same point on the celestial sphere as referenced to the Sun" (NASA StarChild).
It carries the solar system around the centre of our galaxy at an average speed of about "230 km/s (828,000 km/h)" (*Wikipedia*, "Galactic year", citing NASA StarChild, February 2000).

NASA StarChild adds that "it still takes us about 230 million years to make one complete orbit around the Milky Way!" (*Wikipedia* gives "approximately 225 million Earth years", citing Leong 2002.) - **"Nor does the night overtake the day" (36:40).** [Established] Day and night follow each other as the Earth turns; at every moment it is day on one half of the Earth and night on the other. - **The skeptic's point about the hadith.** [Established] Because of the same rotation, the Sun is always setting somewhere and rising somewhere else.
So new moon to new moon is 29.5 days (NASA StarChild).
S7: **Weighing it.** - **"They do not mix" is wrong.** The Mediterranean outflow is strongly mixed by tides at Gibraltar and blends as it moves west (*Wikipedia*).

- Where a river meets the sea, its fresh water can ride over the salt water in a distinct layer (NOAA). - About a million cubic metres of Mediterranean water pour into the Atlantic every second, beneath the incoming Atlantic water (*Wikipedia*). - Lenses of Mediterranean water up to about 100 km across "can survive for many years and can move through thousands of kilometers" (*Wikipedia*).

It exits at about 120 m depth and sinks to an equilibrium depth of about 1,100 m, at a rate of about 1 Sverdrup (a million cubic metres per second) (*Wikipedia*, "Mediterranean outflow"). - **But it does mix.** [Established] At Gibraltar, tides flowing over the Camarinal Sill create "an internal bore", which breaks into internal waves that drive strong mixing; the outflow becomes "less saline due to mixing" as it moves west.

Lenses of Mediterranean water called meddies, with radii of 10–50 km (about 20–100 km across) and 500–1,000 m thick, carry its salt far into the Atlantic; "between 15 and 20 meddies are formed" each year (*Wikipedia*). - **The viral video.** [Established] A widely shared photo said to show "two oceans meeting but not mixing" in the Gulf of Alaska shows, according to Lead Stories, "another river plume taken during a research cruise in the Gulf of Alaska" (photo by Kent Smith, 2010).
Salty, warm Mediterranean water flows out under the Atlantic water flowing in, then sinks to about 1,100 m; tides mix it strongly at the strait (*Wikipedia*).
S11: "Camel urine comes out as a thick syrup, and camel faeces are so dry that they do not require drying when used to fuel fires" (*Wikipedia*).

- A camel can lose a quarter of its body weight in water and survive (*Wikipedia*). - It can drink up to 110 litres in ten minutes (Ali et al. 2023). - Its red blood cells can swell to 240% of their volume without bursting (Ali et al. 2023).

Each point is tied to the verse's "how they are created". - **The hump.** [Established] "The humps in fact are reservoirs of fatty tissue, which can be used as a reserve source of calories, not water" (*Wikipedia*).

In a 2023 study, camels deprived of water for 20 days lost 31% of their initial body weight, from a mean of 363.6 kg to 251.8 kg (Ali et al.). - **Drinking it back.** [Established] Dehydrated camels "can drink up to 110 liters of water within 10 min to restore one-third of their body weight loss", and store "the water for up to 24 h in the gut with slow absorption", so the blood is not suddenly diluted (Ali et al., Introduction). - **Red blood cells.** [Established] "camels' red blood cells are oval rather than circular in shape" (*Wikipedia*), and "The RBCs of the dehydrated camels can swell up to 240% of the initial volume without rupture", against about 150% in other species (Ali et al., Introduction — background, not their own result). - **Saving water.** [Established] Body temperature ranges from "34 °C (93 °F) at dawn" to "40 °C (104 °F) by sunset" (*Wikipedia*), so the camel stores heat by day instead of sweating it away.

In dehydrated camels, hump size shrinks (Ali et al. 2023). - **Surviving water loss.** [Established] "Camels can withstand losing 25% of their body weight in water", while most other mammals tolerate only about 12–14% before circulatory failure (*Wikipedia*).
The sources read give "as much as 30 imperial gallons (140 litres) at a time" (*Wikipedia*) and "up to 110 liters of water within 10 min" (Ali et al.).
Up to about 110 litres in ten minutes after severe dehydration (Ali et al. 2023); *Wikipedia* gives up to 140 litres at a time.
S14: - A stick in the ground is a clock: its shadow tells the time of the afternoon prayer (al-Tirmidhi 149; *Wikipedia*). - The shadow before sunrise, which the commentators saw in this verse, is drawn in gently, not snapped away: "a brief grasp".

For the Maliki, Shafiʿi and Hanbali schools it begins when "the length of any object's shadow equals the length of the object itself plus the length of that object's shadow at noon"; in "the dominant opinion in the Hanafi school", when the shadow "is twice the length of the object plus the length of that object's shadow at noon" (*Wikipedia*, "Asr prayer").
S16: **Weighing it.** - *Roots:* true, and the Airy model's "about five times" supports "several times deeper" (*Wikipedia*). - *"Stabilise the earth":* not in the sense of preventing earthquakes.

- Beneath a high mountain, the crust may reach about 80 km deep, double the average (*Wikipedia*). - In the Airy model, the hidden root is about five times deeper than the mountain is tall (*Wikipedia*). - India is still pushing into Asia by 40–50 mm a year (USGS).

Crust in continental collision zones can reach about 80 km, against about 40 km for average continental crust (*Wikipedia*). - **How the roots were found.** [Established] Plumb lines near the Andes and in India were pulled sideways by mountains "less than expected"; in 1855 George Airy and John Henry Pratt each proposed an explanation: Airy, roots of lighter crust beneath the mountains; Pratt, that the crust under mountains is less dense (*Wikipedia*). - **But mountain belts are earthquake zones.** [Established] The Himalaya formed, and is still forming, as the India and Eurasia plates converge "at a relative rate of 40–50 mm/yr"; "Northward underthrusting of India beneath Eurasia generates numerous earthquakes", making the region "one of the most seismically hazardous regions on Earth" (USGS).

Each point is tied to "stakes" and "firmly set". - **Mountains have roots.** [Established] *Isostasy* is "the state of gravitational equilibrium between Earth's crust (or lithosphere) and mantle": the crust "floats" at a height set by its thickness and density (*Wikipedia*).
In the simple Airy model, mountain "roots will be about five times deeper than the height of the mountains", so an 8 km mountain would have a root about 32 km deep (*Wikipedia*).
Under isostasy, high mountains are balanced by thick roots of lighter crust; in the Airy model, about five times deeper than the mountain is tall (*Wikipedia*).
S19: - **Where iron is made.** [Established] Iron-56, "comprising about 91.754% of the iron on Earth", forms in massive stars: "Among the heavier elements formed is 56Ni, which subsequently decays to 56Co and then 56Fe" (*Wikipedia*).
- Most of Earth's iron is iron-56, made in massive stars from nickel-56 decaying through cobalt (*Wikipedia*). - Iron is the point where fusion in a star stops releasing energy (*Wikipedia*).
Yes: iron-56 forms in massive stars (*Wikipedia*).
S20: - A single ant's alarm is built to reach nestmates up to about 10 cm away (a diffusion model predicts at most about 20 cm), and fades within minutes unless others reinforce it (AntWiki). - Ant colonies have two alarm responses: attack, or the whole colony fleeing (AntWiki).

AntWiki's list of "alarm-defense substances" includes citronellal, dendrolasin, dimethyl sulfate and undecane; formic acid, used by some formicine ants, it calls "probably purely defensive" (AntWiki, from Hölldobler & Wilson). - **How far a warning reaches.** [Established] In the ant *Lasius claviger*, the alarm comes from the Dufour's gland (discharged with the mandibular gland).
Mainly with alarm pheromones, sometimes with sound; the colony may attack or flee (AntWiki).

Unless reinforced, the signal "dies out within a few minutes" (AntWiki). - **Two kinds of alarm.** [Established] "In aggressive alarm some of the colony members… are drawn toward the threatening stimulus"; "In panic alarm the colony as a whole flees from the stimulus" (AntWiki). - **Sound too.** [Established] Some ants add stridulatory chirps, which "enhance attraction" (AntWiki). - **Context matters.** Sasaki, Hölldobler, Millar and Pratt (2014) studied "a context-dependent alarm signal" in *Temnothorax rugatulus* (title; the findings have not yet been consulted).
S24: - **Where our solar system came from.** [Established] The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the "gravitational collapse of a small part of a giant molecular cloud", mostly hydrogen and helium (about 98% of its mass), with about 2% heavier elements; the rest of the collapsing material "flattened into a protoplanetary disk", from which the planets formed (*Wikipedia*).
- Our Sun and planets formed from a cloud of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago (*Wikipedia*). - The four giant planets hold "just under 99% of all the mass orbiting the Sun" (*Wikipedia*).

S33: - The Morpho's blue is made by shape alone; fill the shape with alcohol instead of air and the blue turns greenish (KQED; Kuntzleman). - Most animals cannot make blue pigment at all (KQED). - Human skin colour tracks sunlight closely: a balance between protecting folate and making vitamin D (Jablonski & Chaplin).

Each scale is a single cell, about 50 microns across and 200–250 microns long. - **Blue is rare as a pigment.** [Established] "Blue is one the rarest colors made as a pigment"; "Most animals can't produce blue pigments" (Ryan Null, UC Berkeley, in KQED). - **Change the gaps, change the colour.** [Established] When methanol fills the gaps between a Morpho's scale ridges instead of air, the calculated reflected peak shifts from 452 nm to 545 nm — from blue towards green — because the refractive index of the gaps changes (Kuntzleman, ChemEd X, 2019).

This is "structural color": "the production of color by nano-sized elaborate shapes that reflect and bend light"; ridges on the scales are "a key component" (KQED, quoting the Patel lab, UC Berkeley).
Tiny ridged structures on its scales reflect and bend light (KQED); fill them with methanol and the colour shifts towards green (Kuntzleman).
